title: Symbolic interface elements for children under 3 and ages 3–5
statement:
Symbolic interface elements that adults read effortlessly, such as progress bars and on-screen cartoon-hand gesture demos, were entirely inaccessible to children under 3 in a randomized controlled trial, needed deliberate design for ages 3–5, and became harder (not easier) to understand when decorated with thematic visual detail.

Options:
- Direct progress (under 4): Object-continuity progress: show progress through the items the child manipulates (for example a transparent cup that visibly fills) instead of a separate meter (fits: gentle, nurturing, playful)
- Minimal progress bar: Plain, undecorated, clearly segmented progress bar for ages 4–5 (fits: simple, clean, calm)
- Explain the symbol: Pair any symbol with an explicit statement of the link, such as 'I'll add a star each time you finish a letter!' (fits: warm, guiding, friendly)
- Look-alike symbols: Use symbols that visually resemble what they stand for (a demo hand that looks like a hand and mirrors the gesture) (fits: clear, literal, friendly)
- Direct feedback for toddlers: No symbolic demos for under-3s: replace them with direct cause-and-effect feedback (fits: gentle, simple, nurturing)
appliesWhen: Applies to: kids apps, early learning products, onboarding flows, progress indicators. Audience: children under 10.

source.title: Hidden symbols: How informal symbolism in digital interfaces disrupts usability for preschoolers
source.authors: Alexis Hiniker; Kiley Sobel; Sungsoo (Ray) Hong; Hyewon Suh; India Irish; Julie A. Kientz
